target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday will remove a major scheduling barrier and help people vote more easily
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off from private employers, so low-income retail, food service, and other hourly workers may still be scheduled to work or lose pay if they take time off. That means the holiday may not actually help the people with the biggest voting constraints.

target: AG1’s assumption that turning Election Day into a holiday will make voting broadly accessible because it changes the day’s schedule
objection: Employers still have strong incentives to keep operations running on Election Day, so without a targeted voting-leave requirement, the practical workplace barrier remains for many workers.

target: AG1’s idea that an Election Day holiday is a proven way to increase turnout
objection: Research and experience indicate that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with reforms that directly address access, time, and registration mechanics.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is ineffective because it does not guarantee paid time off
objection: That objection overstates the problem: even without paid leave, a national holiday can reduce scheduling barriers by changing school and workplace defaults, freeing daytime availability for many voters and lowering overall friction.

target: AG2’s claim that not guaranteeing paid leave means the holiday does not really help low-income workers
objection: The relevant barrier is not only lost wages but also time scarcity. A holiday can still improve access by reducing conflicts with school schedules, childcare, errands, commuting, and other daytime obligations.

target: AG2’s preference for state-level time-off laws instead of a federal holiday
objection: A patchwork of state rules can leave many people behind depending on where they live. A national holiday creates a uniform baseline across states rather than uneven protections.

target: AG2’s argument that the policy is ineffective unless paid leave is also mandated
objection: The fact that a holiday should be paired with stronger protections does not make the holiday itself pointless; policy can address both the calendar barrier and the workplace-protection barrier together.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday helps because schools close and many workplaces follow holiday schedules
objection: Private employers are not required to pay workers for the day off, and low-wage service jobs often continue operating, so the people most constrained by work may still not get usable voting time.

target: AG1’s point that a holiday reduces non-wage obligations like school routines and childcare
objection: Those benefits are uneven, because low-income families are less able to absorb the cost of last-minute childcare or lost wages if they still need to work; school closure alone does not create real voting access for them.

target: AG1’s defense of a uniform national holiday as the best way to avoid patchwork access
objection: A federal holiday is a blunt instrument because it changes the calendar without directly changing employer incentives or guaranteeing paid, protected time to vote, whereas targeted employer time-off laws and access reforms address the actual bottleneck.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is ineffective because low-wage workers still may not get guaranteed paid time off
objection: That criticism misses that a holiday can still reduce the day’s overall scheduling disruption: many workplaces scale back on federal holidays, and the changed day timing and routines can make voting easier even without a full day off.

target: AG2’s claim that wage loss and time scarcity are inseparable, so a holiday cannot help
objection: A holiday helps the non-wage side of the problem by reducing school, errand, and commuting friction, making voting feasible even when someone cannot take a full day off work.

target: AG2’s argument that state-level, targeted approaches are better than a holiday
objection: Patchwork state rules can leave millions without access depending on where they live, so a national holiday is valuable as a uniform baseline for civic participation.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is not effective unless paired with a requirement to provide time to vote
objection: That concern does not defeat the holiday itself, because the holiday can be part of a broader policy package that also mandates protected voting time and addresses compensation or job protection.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday still helps by reducing daily disruption even if it does not guarantee pay
objection: For many low-wage jobs, the business does not shut down on holidays, especially in retail, food service, transit, and similar sectors, so the practical need for time during work hours remains unmet by the holiday alone.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday meaningfully helps through reduced routine and childcare burdens
objection: If workers still face lost wages or cannot afford childcare, a calendar change does not turn “more available hours” into real voting access for the people most constrained by employment.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a holiday can be paired with a voting-time mandate to become effective
objection: If the policy only works when combined with a separate requirement to provide time off, then the real policy lever is the time-off protection, not the holiday, so lawmakers should adopt the time-off rule directly instead of changing the national calendar.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is still worthwhile even if not sufficient alone
objection: Calling it “not sufficient alone” does not answer the fact that the holiday itself does not solve the core worker problem, because service and retail jobs still run and people still need protected, paid time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday reduces day-length disruption and therefore helps voters
objection: Day-length disruption does not fix the main barrier for low-wage workers, because holiday staffing often continues in service industries and still conflicts with voting hours.

target: AG1’s point that a holiday lowers school and errand friction for families
objection: The people most constrained by employment are also least able to absorb pay loss or unexpected childcare costs, so a calendar change without protected time does not reliably convert availability into actual voting.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday can be paired with voting-leave protections
objection: If the holiday only works when paired with separate protected-time rules, then the holiday is mostly redundant and adds political and legislative complexity without guaranteeing the needed access.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday effects help everyone without paid leave
objection: A federal holiday can create inequities because service and retail workers may still be required to work; employers can adjust staffing while workers remain exposed to wage loss or reduced flexibility.

target: AG1’s claim that reducing non-wage frictions is enough to justify the holiday
objection: The biggest binding constraint for low-income workers is losing income when they take time off, so calendar relief is not the same as protected, paid time to vote.
